title: sampling-strategy-variance-decomposition-for-bench-harness
content:
Purpose
This note documents a sampling-first approach to throughput harness execution that explicitly decomposes observed variance into (a) client-side scheduling noise, (b) runtime transient behavior (warmup/priming), and (c) steady-state stochasticity. The goal is to produce repeatable throughput estimates and defensible confidence intervals for comparisons across kernel changes, quantization variants, and model sizes.

Why this is different
Many of our existing bench docs focus on warmup timing and occupancy. This doc centers the statistical design: how we sample, how many independent trials to run, and how to attribute variance to instrumentation, arrival patterns, and the serving runtime. The method emphasizes small, independent samples during a validated steady window and bootstrap-based uncertainty.

Definitions and abbreviations
- Trial: one independent execution of the full load profile (including warmup).
- Sample: a single throughput measurement taken over a fixed measurement interval during the trial steady window.
- Steady window: contiguous time range within the trial where system metrics show stationarity (no monotonic drift in throughput or utilization).
- Occupancy: fraction of GPUs/worker slots currently active with at least one batch in flight.
- CV: coefficient of variation (std/mean).

High-level method
1) Design a short warmup to reach operational state (priming). 2) Run N independent trials (N >= 7 recommended, adjustable based on measured variance). 3) From each trial, extract M non-overlapping samples from the validated steady window (M >= 5). 4) Treat the aggregated samples as independent observations for bootstrap CI and variance decomposition. 5) Run an ANOVA-like breakdown to apportion variance to trial-to-trial vs within-trial (client jitter) components.

Why multiple samples per trial?
- Within a single trial the serving runtime can show micro-oscillations due to batching dynamics, KV cache alignment, and transient GC or memory reclamation. Multiple short samples give us an estimate of within-trial variability without requiring many full trials, which are expensive on dedicated fleets.

Recommended experiment parameters (starting point)
- Warmup phase: 120s initial ramp with staircase priming (0.25x -> 0.5x -> 0.75x -> target) holding 15s at each step to allow batch stabilizers to run.
- Trial length: 600s (10 minutes) including warmup.
- Steady window candidate: last 420s of the trial (after the staircase completes).
- Measurement sample interval: 30s non-overlapping windows, produces M = 14 samples per trial.
- Number of independent trials: N = 8 (total samples = 112). Increase N if CV across trials > 0.06 or if p99 latency volatility is high.

Practical loadgen config guidelines
- Use multiple client threads distributed across hosts with pinned CPU affinity to avoid scheduling jitter.
- Use consistent RNG seeds for synthetic prompt selection but allow request arrival jitter (Poisson jitter factor) to emulate production variability.
- Keep token lengths and model context distributions representative of target workload; avoid synthetic uniform short-context samples unless the goal is microbenching.

Metrics to capture per sample
- tokens_per_second (aggregate), requests_per_second, avg_batch_size, p50/p90/p95/p99 latency (server-side), queue_depth_mean, gpu_utilization_mean, cpu_rps, memory_pressure, kv_cache_hit_rate, kernel_rpc_errors.
- Also capture dev-level counters: kernel_launch_rate, small-batch-frequency, continuous-batching-effectiveness.

Diagnostics to mark steady window validity
A steady window is valid if during the candidate window:
- tokens_per_second slope (linear regression) magnitude < 0.005 tokens/s per second (practically flat).
- GPU utilization stddev/mean < 0.03.
- p95 latency trend not increasing monotonically beyond a small tolerance.
If any check fails, truncate earlier or extend the trial. If you cannot identify a flat segment, flag trial as non-stationary and exclude from primary aggregate but keep for root-cause inspection.

Variance decomposition and statistical tests
- Compute per-sample throughput and use a nested variance estimator: total_variance = between_trials_variance + within_trials_variance.
- Use one-way ANOVA on trial means to test whether trial-to-trial differences are significant (alpha = 0.05). If significant, investigate cluster-level causes (node placement, scheduling, background jobs).
- Bootstrap 95% CI: resample samples with replacement at the sample level (not aggregated trial means) to get CI around median and mean throughput. Prefer median when tail latency/presence of outliers is high.
- If comparing two configurations, use a paired test when possible (same seed and trial schedule) or a stratified bootstrap that respects trial structure. Report effect size and whether CI excludes practical equivalence thresholds (e.g., 2% throughput difference).

Client noise isolation steps
- Run a pure client-noise control: with the same client hosts but request the same fixed, degenerate payload that the runtime responds to instantly (a no-op stub). Measure client-side CV. This isolates network and client scheduling variance.
- Subtract estimated client variance from total variance (in quadrature) to approximate runtime-only variance. Document assumptions.

Warmup micro-procedures (practical tips)
- Priming prompts: include at least one prompt that touches maximum sequence length to ensure KV cache warm path exercised.
- Avoid priming with perfectly repeated prompts only; include slight entropy to trigger different attention kernel code paths.
- Between trials: wait 60–120s for resource reclaim and kernel-level cooldown on shared physical nodes. On dedicated fleets, consider a small background flush job to clear caches deterministically.

Failure modes and triage signals
- If p99 spikes only in the first sample of each trial: indicates incomplete priming. Increase warmup time or adjust staircase steps.
- If within-trial samples show multimodal throughput distribution: check if batching window or timer jitter is aligning/disaligning with request flow; instrument batch sizes over time.
- If between-trial variance dominates: look at ephemeral placement differences (e.g., GC, maintenance cron, noisy neighbors) and re-run trials pinned to specific worker IDs.

Reporting template (what to include in PR/bench report)
- Bench config (warmup, trial length, N, M, sample interval)
- Aggregate numbers: median throughput, mean throughput, 95% bootstrap CI, CV, p95/p99 latencies with CIs
- Variance breakdown: between-trial % and within-trial %
- Client-noise control result and adjusted runtime-only throughput estimate
- Observed occupancy and avg batch size distribution plot (attach time-series)
- Any non-stationary trials flagged and rationale for exclusion

Quick checklist before merging a perf PR
- [ ] Run N=8 trials with M>=10 per-trial samples on current baseline and proposed change.
- [ ] Compute bootstrap CI and ensure proposed delta outside CI and > practical threshold (2%).
- [ ] Run client-noise control to ensure improvement isn’t due to client scheduling.
- [ ] Attach time-series traces and batch-size heatmap.

Appendix: example R-style pseudocode for bootstrap of samples
- Collect vector S of all sample throughput values across trials.
- For i in 1..10000: sample_i = sample_with_replacement(S, size=len(S)); compute median_i = median(sample_i).
- CI = percentile(median_i, [2.5, 97.5]).

Notes and next steps
- We should instrument a lightweight trial label propagation across the serving runtime so logs can be grouped by trial ID without manual grep.
- Expand client-side control to include a "synthetic backpressure" run where we artificially delay responses to emulate network tail effects.
- Consider adding an automated validator that checks steady-window heuristics and fails runs that don’t meet stationarity criteria.
